paras: The expulsion of John Dixon from Fremont, Ohio, took place on May 19–20, 1903, when a mob stoned the home of Dixon, a Black ("colored") worker at the Clauss shear plant who had not gone out with its strikers, and drove him from town. His wife and children took refuge in the jail, while Dixon hid overnight and escaped to Norwalk. A short dispatch about the attack ran in papers across the country, and two Southern papers later held it up as evidence of mob violence against Black people in the North.

Dixon was employed at the Clauss shear plant in Fremont, and when its workers struck he stayed on the job. According to a list later compiled by the Memphis Commercial-Appeal, a mob had already stormed the town's jail in an attempt to lynch three Black men charged with murder.

A dispatch dated Fremont, May 20, said that Dixon's home was stoned the night before, a Tuesday, in what it called "an exciting encounter." His wife and children "escaped the fury of the mob by going to jail," and Dixon hid all night. The next day the mob drove him out of Fremont, and he made his way to Norwalk. The dispatch named no member of the mob, gave no estimate of its size and reported no injuries.
No report of arrests or of any official inquiry into the attack appears in the coverage, and none of the reports says whether Dixon or his family returned to Fremont.

Most papers received the story as a brief wire item, printed under a Fremont dateline in the Indianapolis Journal and as "a special to the Bee from Fremont" by way of Toledo in the Salt Lake Herald and the Abilene Weekly Reflector, all on May 21. Headlines ranged from "Driven from Town by a Mob" and "Ohio Negro Driven from Home by a Mob" to "Mob After Negro in Ohio" in Maryland's Democratic Advocate, while South Dakota weeklies on May 29 used "Strikers Drive Negro from Town," naming the strikers as the attackers where the dispatch said only "a mob." By late May weekly news-in-brief columns had reduced the item to a single line saying he was driven out "because he refused to quit work when strikers did," and one such column, in the Grenada Sentinel, placed the episode in Toledo.

In the South the case became material for commentary on the North. On May 30 the Grenada Sentinel wrote that "the negroes have been forced to leave Fremont, Ohio, on account of race hatred and a thirst for revenge," blamed "infuriated hoodlums," and concluded that "the lot of the negro in the North is a hard one." In July the Lafayette Gazette reprinted the Commercial-Appeal's list of "Southern outrages" that occurred in Northern states, Dixon's case among them, and drew from it the hope that the North would stop criticizing the South when it found it "necessary to lynch some black brute."

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal mentioned the episode on May 30 without naming Dixon, setting it beside a white boycott of a Black postmaster at Goza, Mississippi, as proof that "the Afro-American is always when [between] the devil and the deep saa [sea]." Its paragraph followed the wire text closely but said his wife and "three children" fled to the jail; no Black-press report that names Dixon was found.

The Fremont dispatch said Dixon's home was "stoned," while the Toledo Bee version printed in the Salt Lake Herald said it was "destroyed." Whereas the dispatch linked the attack to his staying at work during the strike, the Commercial-Appeal list said he was driven out "because he was on intimate terms with some negroes charged with murder." Only the Grenada Sentinel said that the jail where the family fled "was stormed by the infuriated hoodlums, bent on having a lynching"; the dispatch, the report closest to the event, mentions no attack on the jail, and the Commercial-Appeal list placed a jail storming earlier, against the three murder suspects.

reader.title: Expulsion of John Dixon from Fremont, Ohio
bases: A mob stoned Dixon's home and drove him from Fremont during a strike he had not joined (A3, A4); no one was reported killed or hurt.

Every report traces to one Fremont dispatch, also sent as a Toledo Bee special (A3, A4, A5); the later Southern items (A17, A24) and the Black-press paragraph (A21) are derivative comment, not independent accounts.

accounts.gist: Dixon's home was stoned (or destroyed) the night of May 19 and a mob drove him from town on May 20; he had stayed at work when the Clauss strikers went out; his family went to jail and he escaped to Norwalk.

accounts.label: Grenada Sentinel editorial
accounts.gist: Black people were forced from Fremont by 'race hatred and a thirst for revenge'; the man barely escaped with his life and the jail sheltering his family was stormed by a mob bent on lynching.

accounts.label: Memphis Commercial-Appeal list
accounts.gist: On May 20 Dixon was stoned and driven from home because he was on intimate terms with Black men charged with murder, after a mob had earlier stormed the jail to lynch three suspects.

accounts.label: St. Paul Appeal paragraph
accounts.gist: A Fremont mob drove away a Clauss plant worker whose wife and three children escaped by going to jail; cited as one more case of the Afro-American trapped between hostile sides.

Weekly news-in-brief columns cut it to one line about refusing to quit work, one placing it in Toledo.
The Grenada Sentinel deplored the 'infuriated hoodlums' and said 'the lot of the negro in the North is a hard one', using the case against the North.
The Lafayette Gazette listed it among Northern 'Southern outrages' to argue the North should not criticize Southern lynching of 'some black brute'.
The St. Paul Appeal set it beside a boycott of a Black postmaster as proof the Afro-American is 'between the devil and the deep sea'.
